title: Effect: The Good Parts (Advanced)
subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree
throughline: one Effect forked into a fiber, traced through its lifetime, cancellation, races, and the full Cause of how it finally exits

chapters.title: Structured Concurrency and Fiber Lifetimes
chapters.blurb: Where a forked fiber lives and when it dies, from parent supervision to daemons and scoped lifetimes.

story.title: Structured Concurrency and Fiber Lifetimes
story.subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree

steps.title: Structured Concurrency and Fiber Lifetimes
steps.narration: Every `Effect` runs on a **fiber**. The moment you `fork`, you choose its *lifetime* — and that choice decides whether resources leak.
steps.say: Every Effect runs on a fiber, and the moment you fork one you take on a question: where does it live, and when does it die.
steps.coverSubtitle: Choosing where a forked fiber lives is a resource-safety decision

steps.title: Forking a supervised child
steps.narration: `Effect.fork` starts an effect on a new **child fiber** and returns a `RuntimeFiber<A, E>` handle. The parent can later join or interrupt it.
steps.say: Start with the simplest fork. The parent fiber calls fork on an Effect, which spins up a child fiber and hands back a handle to it.

steps.title: Supervised: dies with its parent
steps.narration: A fiber forked with `Effect.fork` is **parent-supervised**: when the parent completes, the child is interrupted with it. This guarantees *leak-free* lifecycles at any nesting depth.
steps.say: This child is supervised. It is tied to the parent's lifetime, so when the parent finishes, the child is interrupted along with it. No background fiber outlives its caller by accident.

steps.title: forkDaemon: outlives the parent
steps.narration: `Effect.forkDaemon` forks into the **global scope**. The daemon is *not supervised* by its parent — it runs until it finishes naturally or the application shuts down.
steps.say: Sometimes you want a long-running background task that should not die with its caller. forkDaemon detaches the fiber into the global scope, so it keeps running after the parent is gone.

steps.title: forkScoped and forkIn
steps.narration: `Effect.forkScoped` ties a fiber to the enclosing `Scope`; `Effect.forkIn` targets a *captured* scope. The fiber lives until that **Scope** closes — precise, leak-free control.
steps.say: Between those extremes is the scope. forkScoped binds the fiber to an enclosing scope, and forkIn binds it to a scope you captured by hand. The fiber lives exactly until that scope closes.

steps.title: Combining fibers
steps.narration: `Fiber.zip` / `Fiber.zipWith` combine two fibers into one producing *both* results; `Fiber.orElse` provides a **fallback fiber** that runs only if the first fails.
steps.say: Once you hold fiber handles, you can compose them. Fiber zip and zipWith merge two fibers into one that yields both results, while orElse supplies a fallback fiber if the first one fails.

steps.title: Pick the right fork
steps.narration: The lifetime choice is the design: `fork` (supervised) → `forkDaemon` (global) → `forkScoped` / `forkIn` (scoped), then `Fiber.zip` / `Fiber.orElse` to combine. Each is a *resource-safety* decision.
steps.say: So the whole spine is one decision repeated. Fork for a supervised child that dies with you, forkDaemon for the global scope, forkScoped or forkIn to bind a precise lifetime, and zip or orElse to combine the handles. Choosing among them is how you keep resources safe.

chapters.title: The Interruption Model
chapters.blurb: Cooperative, fully asynchronous cancellation that always runs finalizers before a fiber stops.

story.title: The Interruption Model
story.subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree

steps.title: The Interruption Model
steps.narration: Interruption is *cooperative* and **fully asynchronous** — no polling. A stopped fiber still runs every finalizer before it ends.
steps.say: A fiber you no longer need should stop, but stopping safely is the hard part. Effect's interruption always runs your finalizers first.
steps.coverSubtitle: Cooperative cancellation that always runs your cleanup

steps.title: Requesting interruption
steps.narration: The caller holds a fiber handle. `Fiber.interrupt(fiber)` requests cancellation of a **target fiber** — here one parked in an `Effect.sleep` loop.
steps.say: The calling fiber holds a handle to a target that is busy in a sleep loop. To cancel it, the caller runs Fiber interrupt on that handle.

steps.title: Asynchronous, not polling
steps.narration: Effect uses **asynchronous interruption**, not polling. A fiber can be stopped at any interruptible point; critical sections temporarily *disable* interruptibility to complete atomically.
steps.say: This signal is fully asynchronous. The target does not sit in a loop checking a flag. It can be stopped at any safe point, and a critical section can temporarily disable interruptibility to finish atomically.

steps.title: Finalizers always run
steps.narration: `Effect.onInterrupt` registers cleanup that runs **only on cancellation**. Interruption safely runs *all* finalizers, so resources are released even when work is abandoned.
steps.say: Before the target dies, its cleanup runs. onInterrupt registers an effect that fires only on cancellation, so resources close even when the work is abandoned.

steps.title: Wiring native cancellation
steps.narration: `Effect.async` lets you return a *cleanup effect* or wire an `AbortSignal`, connecting interruption to **native cancellation** — aborting a `fetch`, a timer, or a subscription.
steps.say: For work that lives outside Effect, async bridges the gap. Its cleanup effect, or an AbortSignal, wires native cancellation so a fetch or a timer is aborted when the fiber is interrupted.

steps.title: An Exit with an Interrupt cause
steps.narration: `Fiber.interrupt` **back-pressures** until the fiber terminates, then returns an `Exit` whose cause is `Cause.Interrupt` with a `FiberId`. `Fiber.interruptFork` does it in the *background*.
steps.say: Finally the interrupt resolves. Fiber interrupt back-pressures, waiting for the fiber to fully terminate, then returns an Exit whose cause is an Interrupt carrying the fiber's identity. Interrupt fork does the same in the background without waiting.

steps.title: Self-interrupt and disconnect
steps.narration: `Effect.interrupt` models **self-interruption**; `Effect.disconnect` detaches an *uninterruptible* task so an outer interrupt returns promptly while it finishes independently.
steps.say: Two more tools round it out. Effect interrupt models a fiber cancelling itself, and disconnect detaches an uninterruptible task so interruption of the whole returns promptly while that task winds down on its own.

chapters.title: Racing and Coordination Primitives
chapters.blurb: Resolving the first winner and gating many fibers with PubSub, semaphores, and latches.

story.title: Racing and Coordination Primitives
story.subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree

steps.title: Racing and Coordination Primitives
steps.narration: Beyond forking: **racing** picks a first winner and interrupts the rest; coordination primitives gate *which* fibers may proceed.
steps.say: Concurrency is not just spawning fibers. It is deciding who wins a race and who is allowed to proceed.
steps.coverSubtitle: Resolve the first winner and gate many fibers

steps.title: Race to the first success
steps.narration: `Effect.race(a, b)` resolves with the **first success** and *interrupts the loser*. `Effect.raceAll` races a whole collection.
steps.say: From a generator you race two effects. Race resolves with the first one to succeed and immediately interrupts the loser, so no work is wasted on the result you discarded.

steps.title: raceFirst, raceWith, either
steps.narration: `Effect.raceFirst` returns whichever *completes* first; `Effect.raceWith` supplies per-`Exit` finishers. Wrapping in `Effect.either` reports first completion as `Left`/`Right`.
steps.say: There are sharper variants. raceFirst returns whichever completes first, success or failure. raceWith supplies per-exit finishers for each side. And wrapping each side in either lets a race report the first completion as a Left or a Right instead of failing.

steps.title: PubSub broadcasts to all
steps.narration: `PubSub.bounded` broadcasts each message to *every* subscriber via `PubSub.subscribe` / `PubSub.publish` — unlike a queue. **Subscribe before publishing**, or a subscriber misses the message.
steps.say: Coordination starts with broadcasting. A bounded PubSub sends every published message to every current subscriber, unlike a queue where each value goes to just one. The catch is timing: subscribe before you publish.

steps.title: Semaphore gates concurrency
steps.narration: `Effect.makeSemaphore(n)` issues **permits**; `withPermits(k)` runs an effect once `k` are free, then releases them. *One permit* forces sequential execution — a mutex.
steps.say: To limit how many fibers run at once, reach for a semaphore. makeSemaphore hands out permits, and withPermits acquires the count an effect needs and releases them when it finishes. One permit makes the work strictly sequential.

steps.title: Latch: a one-time gate
steps.narration: `Effect.makeLatch` is a one-time gate. Fibers `await` while it is closed; a single `open` releases all of them. `release` lets waiters pass without permanently opening.
steps.say: Finally a latch is a one-time gate. It starts closed, fibers wait at it on await, and a single call to open releases all of them at once, perfect for blocking work until setup finishes.

steps.title: The coordination toolkit
steps.narration: The full toolkit: `Effect.race` (first winner) → `PubSub` (broadcast) → `Semaphore` (cap concurrency) → `Latch` (one-time gate). Each controls *how fibers coordinate*.
steps.say: Together these are the coordination toolkit. Race for the first winner, PubSub to broadcast, a semaphore to cap concurrency, and a latch to open the gate once setup is done. Each one shapes how your fibers meet.

chapters.title: The Full Failure Tree: Cause and Exit
chapters.blurb: Every way a fiber can end, captured as a Cause tree and surfaced through Exit.

story.title: The Full Failure Tree: Cause and Exit
story.subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree

steps.title: The Full Failure Tree: Cause and Exit
steps.narration: The `E` channel is only the *expected* errors. Effect preserves the **full** failure picture in `Cause<E>` and surfaces it through `Exit`.
steps.say: The error channel only tells you part of the story. Effect keeps the whole picture in a structure called Cause.
steps.coverSubtitle: Every way a fiber can end, including defects and interrupts

steps.title: Beyond the E channel
steps.narration: `Effect.exit` turns an `Effect<A, E, R>` into its `Exit`; `Effect.cause` exposes the underlying `Cause`. Both capture *more* than the `E` channel alone.
steps.say: An Effect can end in more ways than its error type admits. To see them all, exit converts the effect into its outcome, and cause exposes the underlying failure detail directly.

steps.title: Exit is Success or Failure
steps.narration: `Exit<A, E>` is `Success(value)` or `Failure(Cause)` — conceptually `Either<A, Cause<E>>`, but *richer*: the failure side is a full `Cause`, not a bare `E`.
steps.say: An Exit has just two shapes. Success carries a value, and Failure carries a Cause. Think of it as an Either of a value or a Cause, but richer, because the Cause holds far more than a plain error.

steps.title: The leaf causes
steps.narration: The leaf causes: `Fail<E>` (a *typed* error), `Die` (an unexpected **defect**), and `Interrupt` (a cancellation carrying a `FiberId`).
steps.say: A Cause is a tree, and its leaves are the three ways a single fiber can fail. Fail holds a typed, expected error. Die holds a defect, an unexpected bug. And Interrupt records a cancellation along with the fiber's identity.

steps.title: Sequential and Parallel causes
steps.narration: `Sequential` combines two causes that occurred *in order* (e.g. an effect plus a failing finalizer); `Parallel` combines *concurrent* failures. The tree never discards a failure.
steps.say: Because fibers run together, failures can stack. Sequential combines two causes that happened one after another, like an effect failing and then its finalizer failing too. Parallel combines two that failed concurrently. So the tree never loses a single failure.

steps.title: Inspecting the Cause
steps.narration: `Cause.match` branches on shape; `Cause.pretty` formats it; `Cause.failures` / `Cause.defects` extract errors vs bugs. Guards `Cause.isFailType` / `Cause.isDie` classify a node.
steps.say: To work with all this, Cause gives you tools. match branches on the shape of the tree, pretty formats it for logs, and failures and defects pull out the typed errors and the bugs separately. Guards like isFailType and isDie let you classify a single node.

steps.title: Sandbox the whole Cause
steps.narration: `Effect.sandbox` lifts the whole `Cause` into `E` so `catchTags` can handle `Fail`/`Die`/`Interrupt`; `Effect.unsandbox` restores it. `Effect.matchCauseEffect` handles the cause inline. *Nothing is discarded.*
steps.say: And when you want ordinary handlers to see all of it, sandbox lifts the entire Cause into the error channel, so catchTags can match on Fail, Die, and Interrupt by name. Unsandbox restores the original shape, and matchCauseEffect handles the cause inline. Effect never throws failure information away.

chapters.title: Defects, Sandboxing, and Error Accumulation
chapters.blurb: Promoting failures to defects, recovering at boundaries, and collecting many errors instead of failing fast.

story.title: Defects, Sandboxing, and Error Accumulation
story.subtitle: Fibers, interruption, racing, and the full failure tree

steps.title: Defects, Sandboxing, and Error Accumulation
steps.narration: Two final moves: treat unrecoverable bugs as **defects**, and *accumulate* many errors instead of failing fast.
steps.say: Some failures are bugs you never meant to recover from, and some workloads need every error, not just the first. This chapter handles both.
steps.coverSubtitle: Handle unexpected bugs and collect multiple failures

steps.title: Defects are not in E
steps.narration: A **defect** is an unrecoverable bug *not* tracked in `E`. Raise one with `Effect.die(error)` or `Effect.dieMessage("...")`.
steps.say: Start with defects. A defect is an unrecoverable bug, and it is deliberately not tracked in the error channel. You raise one with die, or with dieMessage when you just want a message.

steps.title: Promoting failures to defects
steps.narration: `Effect.orDie` promotes a typed failure to a **defect** — `E` becomes `never`. `Effect.orDieWith` maps the error *before* promoting it.
steps.say: You can also promote an existing failure. orDie turns a typed error into a defect, which empties the error channel to never. orDieWith maps the error first if you want to reshape it on the way.

steps.title: Recover only at boundaries
steps.narration: `Effect.catchAllDefect` / `Effect.catchSomeDefect` recover defects *only at boundaries*. Guards `Cause.isDieType` / `Cause.isRuntimeException` classify the defect you caught.
steps.say: Defects are not meant to be caught everywhere, but at a boundary you sometimes must. catchAllDefect recovers from any defect, catchSomeDefect from selected ones, and the Cause guards like isDie and isRuntimeException let you classify what you caught.

steps.title: Parallel and Sequential causes
steps.narration: Concurrent failures from `Effect.all([...], { concurrency })` combine into a `Parallel` cause; a failing `Effect.ensuring` finalizer yields a `Sequential` cause.
steps.say: How failures combine depends on how they ran. When all runs several effects concurrently and more than one fails, those errors merge into a Parallel cause. A failing finalizer attached with ensuring instead produces a Sequential cause.

steps.title: Fail fast by default
steps.narration: By default `Effect.all` / `Effect.forEach` **short-circuit** — they stop at the *first* error and return it, abandoning the rest.
steps.say: By default, combining effects fails fast. all and forEach stop at the very first error and return it, discarding the work that had not failed yet. Often that is exactly what you want.

steps.title: Accumulate every error
steps.narration: To *accumulate*, map each effect through `Effect.either` or `Effect.option` so failures become values. Now nothing short-circuits — **every** error is collected.
steps.say: But when you need every error, you change the shape instead of the policy. Map each effect through either or option so failures become values, and now nothing short-circuits. Every error is collected alongside every success.
